clue.text: 5 for one who is 9 12?

blocks.note: surface reading: the answer to 5, a photographer or a turtle, standing in for someone
setter's reading: a snapper for a person who is all fingers, so a picture-taker that is fingers-based

explanation.surface: A cross-reference puzzle: a snapper suited to someone who is hopelessly clumsy.
explanation.walkthrough: SNAPPER (5) is a camera; DIGITAL means of the fingers, and someone ALL FINGERS AND THUMBS (9, 12) is all digits. So the clumsy person's snapper is a DIGITAL CAMERA.
explanation.definitionFit: A digital camera is an electronic picture-taking device, and digital also means relating to fingers, the clumsy person's trouble.

clue.text: Graphic indicator thus found in the divine fluid

indicators.note: something found in a place sits inside it, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: ichor is the fluid that ran in the veins of the Greek gods
so means thus, in that way

explanation.surface: Something drawn as a pointer turns up in holy liquid.
explanation.walkthrough: In Greek myth ichor, not blood, flowed in the veins of the gods; an isochor is a term from physics graphs.
explanation.definitionFit: An isochor is a line on a graph joining points of equal volume, so it is a plotted indicator on a chart.

clue.text: Man following some subconscious speech pattern

indicators.note: following means coming after, so the first-named piece goes second

blocks.note: the id is the part of the mind holding unconscious drives, some of the subconscious
IOM is the abbreviation for the Isle of Man

explanation.surface: A man trails along behind some buried mental habit of talking.
explanation.walkthrough: Man is not a person but the Isle of Man, abbreviated IOM, placed after ID.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom is a fixed expression whose meaning is not literal, a characteristic turn of phrase in a language.

clue.text: How stands the defendant?

blocks.note: surface reading: asking about the defendant's position or prospects in a trial
setter's reading: what state is the defendant in, namely charged with a crime

explanation.walkthrough: The question sounds like asking how the case is going; the answer is the defendant's formal status, and is also the very name given to the defendant.
explanation.definitionFit: A defendant stands formally charged with an offence, and in court is called the accused.

clue.text: Traveller with prospects turning turtle

blocks.note: first meaning: a tourist taking photographs of views, prospects being scenic outlooks
second meaning: a snapping turtle, a large aggressive freshwater species

explanation.surface: A traveller with good prospects comes to grief, turning turtle as a boat capsizes.
explanation.walkthrough: Prospects here are views, not career chances, and turning turtle (capsizing) only dresses up the second meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: A snapper is slang for a photographer, such as a holidaymaker capturing views, and also the name of a biting turtle.

clue.text: Marshal bar members into close

indicators.note: the members of a word are its letters taken as a loose group, in any order
going into something puts it inside, so one piece sits within the other

blocks.note: Michel Ney was one of Napoleon's marshals
taken as written

explanation.surface: Organise the people of the legal profession in a confined space.
explanation.walkthrough: Marshal looks like the verb to arrange, but it names one of Napoleon's marshals; the rearranging is signalled by members, the letters of a word.
explanation.definitionFit: As adverb or adjective, nearby and close both mean at a short distance away.

clue.text: Open one's heart ultimately - to a Max Clifford?

indicators.note: ultimately means at the end, so only the final letter of the word is kept

blocks.note: open, as in not secret, is public
one's read as one is, with I for one
the last letter of heart

explanation.surface: Confessing your feelings to a notorious celebrity press agent, who might sell the story.
explanation.walkthrough: Max Clifford was a well-known British PR man who brokered tabloid stories; the question mark marks him as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: Max Clifford was a famous publicity agent, so he is an example of someone who promotes clients in the press.

clue.text: Old electricians love to oppose change, naturally

indicators.note: to oppose is to face the other way, so the run of letters is turned back to front

blocks.note: the ETU was the Electrical Trades Union, merged away long ago
taken as written

explanation.surface: Traditional electrical workers' union members, being conservative, resist change.
explanation.walkthrough: ETU + LOVE is reversed whole: EVOL + UTE.
explanation.definitionFit: Evolute is an old verb meaning to evolve, that is to develop gradually by natural processes.

clue.text: Alters with fumbling hands; altered with fumbling hands

blocks.note: first reading: a verb phrase, someone who handles everything, every item being pawed and leafed through
second reading: describing a person made clumsy, whose hands will not work properly

explanation.walkthrough: Read as a sentence, the phrase says everything gets fingered and thumbed, which is how a clumsy person alters things; read as an adjective it describes that person.
explanation.definitionFit: Being all fingers and thumbs is an idiom for clumsiness with the hands, as if a person had nothing but digits.

clue.text: Good old British infantry starts to desert

indicators.note: starts are beginnings, so only the opening letters of the words are kept

blocks.note: G is the abbreviation for good
O is the abbreviation for old
the first letters of British and infantry

explanation.surface: Soldiers of a fine old regiment begin to go absent without leave.
explanation.walkthrough: Desert looks like the verb, run away, as the surface needs; it is the noun.
explanation.definitionFit: The Gobi is a vast dry region straddling Mongolia and northern China, one of the world's great deserts.

clue.text: Where wines are put down in volume

definitions.text: Where wines are put down in volume

blocks.clueFragment: Where wines are put down in volume
blocks.note: surface reading: a place where wines are laid down for keeping in large quantity
setter's reading: written down in a volume, that is recorded in a book

explanation.walkthrough: In volume seems to mean in bulk, pointing at a cellar; a volume is a book, and put down means written in it.
explanation.definitionFit: A cellar book is a ledger in which a household or merchant records the wines stored in its cellar.

clue.text: See 9
Ribald French verses from Bali you say, translated in transmitted copy

indicators.note: say signals that a word is only spoken, giving the letter with that sound
translating changes the form of words, so these letters are reordered
in places one piece inside the other

blocks.note: taken as written
the letter U is pronounced like the word you
a fax is a copy of a document sent down a telephone line

explanation.surface: Bawdy French poems from Bali, rendered into another language and faxed over.
explanation.walkthrough: Fabliaux are medieval French comic tales in verse, often coarse; the X ending is the French plural.
explanation.definitionFit: Fabliaux are short, often bawdy, comic verse tales of medieval France, so ribald French poems.

clue.text: Fall back north and point out justification

indicators.note: out means outside, so this piece goes round the others

blocks.note: to recede is to fall back or withdraw
N is the abbreviation for north
PT is the abbreviation for point

explanation.surface: Retreat northwards and indicate the reason for doing so.
explanation.walkthrough: Point out looks like a single verb, to indicate; split it, and out means outside, wrapping the abbreviation for point around the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: A precedent is an earlier case cited as authority, so it serves as justification for a present decision.

clue.text: Bent hairstylist's reign of terror?

blocks.note: bent is slang for crooked, criminal, pointing to crime
a wave is a hairstylist's curl set in the hair

explanation.surface: A crooked hairdresser terrorises the neighbourhood.
explanation.walkthrough: Bent is British slang for corrupt or criminal.
explanation.definitionFit: A crime wave is a sudden surge of offences in an area, loosely a period of terror, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Work of 18 having spacecraft without directions

indicators.note: without in its old sense means outside, so this piece goes round the other

blocks.note: Mir was the Soviet and Russian space station
S and E, south and east, are compass directions

explanation.surface: A play by a writer features a spaceship with no sense of direction.
explanation.walkthrough: Without seems to mean lacking, but here it means outside, so the spacecraft goes round the directions.
explanation.definitionFit: The Miser (L'Avare) is a comedy written by Moliere, the answer to 18, so it is one of his works.

clue.text: Stratagem fails to gain entry to sphere of influence

indicators.note: failing to get the first letter of gain means that opening letter is lost

blocks.note: a gambit is an opening ploy or stratagem

explanation.surface: A cunning plan to break into a rival's territory comes to nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: The entry of gain is its first letter G, which GAMBIT fails to keep.
explanation.definitionFit: An ambit is the scope or extent of something, the range over which power or authority reaches.

clue.text: He wrote 'A Man for all Seasons' without exaggeration

indicators.note: without in its old sense means outside, so one piece wraps round the other

blocks.note: A Man for All Seasons is Robert Bolt's play about Sir Thomas More
an exaggeration is a kind of lie or untruth

explanation.surface: Claims a dramatist wrote a well-known historical play, told plainly.
explanation.walkthrough: The play's title stands for its hero, MORE, and without means outside, not lacking.
explanation.definitionFit: Moliere was the great seventeenth-century French comic playwright, so he is a man who wrote.

clue.text: Might 'elp to seal with this?

indicators.note: might suggests a possible version, so these letters could be set out another way

blocks.note: the letters of the dropped-aitch help, to and seal

explanation.surface: A cockney asks whether this would help to close a package.
explanation.walkthrough: Sellotape is the British brand of clear sticky tape. The whole clue is both the wordplay and a description of what it does.
explanation.definitionFit: Sellotape is adhesive tape used for sealing envelopes and parcels, so it is a thing you might close with.

clue.text: Hannibal, born to take the stand

blocks.note: Hannibal Lecter is the cannibal killer of The Silence of the Lambs
N is the abbreviation for born, from French ne

explanation.surface: The fictional serial killer, having been born, is called to give evidence in court.
explanation.walkthrough: Hannibal suggests the Carthaginian general; it is the film killer, and take the stand is a courtroom phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: A lectern is a reading desk with a sloping top, a stand used for holding books in church or lecture hall.

clue.text: Swimmer rushed into a hip replacement

indicators.note: into puts one piece inside another
a replacement puts things in new positions, so these letters are reordered

blocks.note: ran means rushed, moved quickly
taken as written

explanation.surface: A patient hurried into hospital for surgery on the hip joint.
explanation.walkthrough: Swimmer is not a person but a fish.
explanation.definitionFit: The piranha is a South American freshwater fish with sharp teeth, so a swimmer in the crossword sense.

clue.text: 15 over a one-time kingdom

indicators.note: over can mean overturned or upset, so these letters are knocked into a new order

blocks.note: the first word of the answer to 15
taken as written

explanation.surface: A wave of lawlessness overwhelms a former realm.
explanation.walkthrough: 15 points at CRIME WAVE, and only its first word is used here.
explanation.definitionFit: Mercia was an Anglo-Saxon kingdom of the English Midlands, long since absorbed, so a former realm.

clue.text: So Clouseau's no cruciverbalist?

blocks.note: surface reading: the bumbling French detective of the Pink Panther films, who never finds the evidence
setter's reading: a crossword-maker with nothing to write for the solvers

explanation.surface: Inspector Clouseau would make a hopeless crossword compiler.
explanation.walkthrough: The word works for both: a hopeless detective lacks evidence, and a compiler's puzzle would have nothing to solve by.
explanation.definitionFit: Clueless means without any idea, an inept person, and literally lacking the hints a puzzle setter writes.

clue.text: See 1
Queen's speech?

blocks.note: surface reading: the monarch's annual address opening Parliament
setter's reading: a queen is a female cat, so this is the noise she makes

explanation.walkthrough: The Queen's Speech is the British monarch's address setting out the government's programme; a queen is also a female cat.
explanation.definitionFit: Miaow is the cry a cat utters, so it is how a female cat talks.

clue.text: Revival of the kidneys not left to science: not one!

indicators.note: not left says the letter standing for left is taken out
not one says the letter standing for one is removed

blocks.note: renal means relating to the kidneys
taken as written

explanation.surface: The kidneys' recovery isn't left to medicine: none of it!
explanation.walkthrough: RENAL drops L (left), SCIENCE drops I (one), and the pair join.
explanation.definitionFit: Renascence is rebirth or renewal, a coming back to life, which is what revival means.

clue.text: Sally's so shy

blocks.note: surface reading: a girl called Sally is very timid
setter's reading: to shy is to throw, and Sally's companion word names a fairground figure pelted with balls

explanation.walkthrough: An Aunt Sally is a fairground figure people throw things at, hence a target of abuse; the answer is the word that goes with Sally, so shy here is to throw.
explanation.definitionFit: Aunt is the word completing the name Aunt Sally, the traditional target that fairgoers throw sticks or balls at.

clue.text: Warhorse needing surgeon at near-disaster

indicators.note: a disaster wrecks things, leaving these letters in a jumble

blocks.note: a vet is an animal surgeon
taken as written

explanation.surface: A horse in battle, close to catastrophe, needs an animal doctor.
explanation.walkthrough: Warhorse looks like a cavalry mount needing the vet, but means a seasoned old campaigner.
explanation.definitionFit: A warhorse is figuratively an old soldier or long-serving campaigner, which a veteran is.

clue.text: Lewis Eliot, say, put up with the cold

blocks.note: first meaning: Lewis Eliot is the narrator of C. P. Snow's novel sequence
second meaning: a figure built in winter weather from packed flakes

explanation.surface: A fictional character tolerates the chilly weather.
explanation.walkthrough: Put up with looks like tolerate; it means built, along with the cold.
explanation.definitionFit: C. P. Snow created Lewis Eliot in his Strangers and Brothers novels, and a snowman is a figure built in freezing weather.
